\item \emph{Probability to mean.} If \(X_n\to X\) in probability, then
      \(X_n\to X\) in \(L^p\) if and only if \(X_n\in L^p\) for every
      \(n\) and \((|X_n|^p)_{n\geq1}\) is uniformly integrable
      (\cref{thm:p15-w02b-p15-013-vitali}).
text:
\item \emph{Probability to mean.} Let \(X_n\to X\) in probability.
      If \(X_n\in L^p\) for every \(n\), then \(X_n\to X\) in
      \(L^p\) if and only if \((|X_n|^p)_{n\geq1}\) is uniformly
      integrable (\cref{thm:p15-w02b-p15-013-vitali}). Without that
      hypothesis, \(X_n\to X\) in \(L^p\) if and only if some tail
      \((|X_n-X|^p)_{n\geq N}\) consists of integrable variables and is
      uniformly integrable; the condition ``\(X_n\in L^p\) for every
      \(n\) and \((|X_n|^p)_{n\geq1}\) uniformly integrable'' is then
      sufficient but not necessary, as \(X_n=X=Y\) with
      \(\mathbb E|Y|^p=\infty\) shows
      (\cref{thm:p15-w02c-p15-014-probability-mean}).

anchor_quote:
This is a lambda-system: it contains \(\Omega\), equality for a complement
follows by subtraction from the total integrals, and equality for a
countable disjoint union follows from dominated convergence of its
finite-union indicators, dominated separately by \(|X_\infty|\) and \(|Z|\).
text:
This is a lambda-system in the sense of \cref{def:p15-pi-lambda};
each defining condition is checked directly. First, \(\Omega\) belongs to every
sigma-algebra \(\mathcal F_n\), and the integrals of \(X_\infty\) and
\(Z\) agree on every member of \(\bigcup_n\mathcal F_n\), so
\(\Omega\in\mathcal L\). Second, let \(A\subseteq B\) be members of
\(\mathcal L\). Since \(\mathbf 1_{B\setminus A}=\mathbf 1_B-\mathbf 1_A\)
and \(X_\infty\) and \(Z\) are integrable, all four integrals below are
finite and
\[
 \int_{B\setminus A}X_\infty\,dP=\int_B X_\infty\,dP-\int_A X_\infty\,dP
 =\int_B Z\,dP-\int_A Z\,dP=\int_{B\setminus A}Z\,dP,
\]
so \(B\setminus A\in\mathcal L\). Third, let \(B_k\in\mathcal L\) with
\(B_k\subseteq B_{k+1}\) and \(B=\bigcup_k B_k\). Then
\(\mathbf 1_{B_k}X_\infty\to\mathbf 1_B X_\infty\) pointwise with
\(|\mathbf 1_{B_k}X_\infty|\leq|X_\infty|\), and likewise for \(Z\) with
bound \(|Z|\); dominated convergence gives
\(\int_{B_k}X_\infty\,dP\to\int_B X_\infty\,dP\) and
\(\int_{B_k}Z\,dP\to\int_B Z\,dP\). The two sequences are equal term by
term, so their limits agree and \(B\in\mathcal L\). Finally
\(B\in\mathcal F_\infty\) in the second and third steps because
\(\mathcal F_\infty\) is a sigma-algebra.

anchor_quote: If \(\sup_i E\Phi(|X_i|)<\infty\), the family is uniformly integrable.
text:
Let \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) be real random variables, with no integrability
assumed. If \(\sup_i E\Phi(|X_i|)<\infty\), every \(X_i\) is integrable and
the family is uniformly integrable.
